issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: For intimate partner physical abuse, 'being forced to do something' and tactile body-state cues are plausible triggers, but 'burnt smell' introduces a danger cue more typical of fire/explosion trauma and is not supported by the other selected items. It feels disconnected from the stated trauma and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal pattern is otherwise self-blaming/defectiveness-focused and tightly linked to triggers, but 'fear of rage' shifts to fear of one's own future violent loss of control. That theme is not supported by the trauma type, the other appraisals, or the maladaptive strategies, making this item difficult to integrate into the same formulation.

issues.item: Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time; Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
issues.explanation: The memory items indicate highly severe, here-and-now re-experiencing, which is plausible at this PCL-5 level, but they sit awkwardly with the formulation because Memory has only a weak link to Negative Appraisals and no active links to Triggers or Maladaptive Strategies. Selecting two very strong reliving items plus disorganized narration makes Memory appear more central than the formulation suggests.

vignette: Lena, a 35-year-old South Eastern Asian woman and married physical therapist, has struggled with the aftermath of severe physical abuse inflicted by her romantic partner. The event, which occurred several months ago, has left an indelible mark on her life, affecting both her personal relationships and professional duties. The traumatic event itself was a violent episode that Lena still vividly recalls. Her husband had grown increasingly agitated and physically abusive after a heated argument over family matters. When he touched her in anger, the sensation of his hands gripping her arm sent waves of panic through her body. She felt an overwhelming loss of autonomy as she was forced to endure his aggressive actions. The memory of that night still feels present and raw, as if it were happening all over again. In the days following the incident, Lena found herself dwelling on how she used to be before the event-a more confident and self-assured person. She became hypervigilant around others, always scanning for signs of potential danger in people's demeanor or actions. This constant vigilance was fueled by the overwhelming sense that she somehow brought this upon herself. The memory would flood back at unexpected moments, leaving her unable to explain clearly what had happened. When the memory returned, she felt so emotionally overwhelmed that she often had to stop whatever she was doing and retreat into a safe space. Lena's hypervigilance towards people led her to be extremely wary of any physical contact, including those from colleagues at work or even her husband's innocent gestures. Any touch would trigger memories of the abuse, causing her to withdraw quickly. This avoidance behavior became so pronounced that she found it difficult to maintain professional relationships with her patients and coworkers. The memory's overwhelming nature further exacerbated Lena's negative appraisals about herself. She was certain that there was something fundamentally wrong with her as a person, and the feeling of permanent humiliation lingered constantly in the back of her mind. These beliefs led her to dwell on how the event could have been prevented, which only deepened her self-blame and sense of defectiveness. Lena's negative appraisals not only fueled her hypervigilance but also triggered more intense reactions when she encountered specific temperatures or felt forced into situations against her will. This cycle became increasingly self-reinforcing: as she continued to blame herself for the event, she found it harder to cope with triggers in daily life. Over time, these patterns began to affect Lena's professional duties significantly. She had trouble maintaining close physical contact during therapy sessions and often needed breaks from work due to emotional exhaustion. Her husband noticed her withdrawal and growing anxiety but did not understand the full extent of what she was experiencing. The combination of self-blame, hypervigilance, and vivid memories led Lena to finally seek help. She recognized that without support, her quality of life would continue to diminish. Lena is most afraid of being unable to reclaim a sense of normalcy in her personal and professional life. However, she also holds onto hope that with the right guidance, she can start healing and regain control over her experiences. In therapy, Lena will need to address these interlocking cycles of triggers, maladaptive strategies, memory disturbances, and negative appraisals to break free from this tightening loop and find a way forward.
